title: Fibres of the affine groupoid invariant spectrum are orbits
statement: Let $U=\operatorname{Spec}A$ and $R=\operatorname{Spec}B$ be affine schemes [def-pc-scheme], [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Suppose $s,t:R\to U$, $e:U\to R$, $i:R\to R$ and $c:R\times_{s,U,t}R\to R$ [def-pc-fibre-product] are morphisms such that, functorially in every test scheme $H$, $U(H)$ is the object set and $R(H)$ the arrow set of a groupoid with source $s$, target $t$, identity $e$, inverse $i$ and composition $c$. Write $\sigma=s^\sharp,\tau=t^\sharp:A\to B$ and $C=\{a\in A:\sigma(a)=\tau(a)\}$. Assume $s,t$ are finite locally free [def-pc-finite-locally-free]. For $M=\operatorname{Spec}C$, the canonical map $|U|\to|M|$ is surjective. Two points $u_0,u_1\in|U|$ have the same image in $|M|$ if and only if there exists $r\in|R|$ with $s(r)=u_0$ and $t(r)=u_1$. Moreover, for every algebraically closed field $k$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure], the map $U(k)\to M(k)$ is surjective and its fibres are exactly the equivalence classes generated by $s,t:R(k)\rightrightarrows U(k)$.

proof.text: Apply [lem-a1-affine-groupoid-integral-invariants] with the given groupoid: $C\hookrightarrow A$ is integral. It is injective because $C$ is the displayed subring of $A$. Lying over [lem-weil-pbc-integral-injective-lying-over] therefore gives a prime of $A$ over every prime of $C$, proving surjectivity of $|U|\to|M|$. This includes $A=0$, when both spectra are empty.

Fix an algebraically closed field $k$ and a map $c:C\to k$. Put $\mathfrak p=\ker c$. Lying over supplies $\mathfrak q\subset A$ over $\mathfrak p$. The map $c$ extends to $\kappa(\mathfrak p)\to k$ by sending a fraction to the quotient of its images. By [lem-a1-integral-residue-extension-algebraic], $\kappa(\mathfrak q)/\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ is algebraic. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-algebraic-extension-embeds-algebraically-closed] to extend that embedding to $\kappa(\mathfrak q)\to k$. Composing $A\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)\to k$ lifts $c$. The affine spectrum correspondence identifies this with a $k$-point of $U$ over the prescribed $k$-point of $M$.

To compare two lifts $a_0,a_1:A\to k$ of $c$, form $A'=A\otimes_C k$, $B'=B\otimes_C k$ and $\sigma',\tau':A'\to B'$. The affine tensor-product base-change formula [lem-sbc-finite-affine-tensor-base-change], with one summand, identifies these with the schemes obtained by base change from $M$ to $\operatorname{Spec}k$. The structure maps are over $M$: the two maps from $R$ agree on $C$; also $s\circ e=t\circ e=1$, inversion interchanges $s,t$, and composition preserves the common $M$-image. Thus their base changes satisfy the same groupoid identities. The maps $a_j$ extend to $k$-algebra maps $\alpha_j:A'\to k$, $\alpha_j(a\otimes\lambda)=a_j(a)\lambda$. Finite, flat, and locally finite presentation are separately preserved by arbitrary base change by the three cited permanence statements, so $s',t'$ satisfy exactly the finite locally free definition. On each local free norm chart, tensoring a basis gives a basis over the new ring. This also gives the chartwise multiplication matrices used below.

Use the norm sections of [lem-pd-finite-locally-free-norm-charts]. Their compatibility with scalar extension is a direct determinant calculation: on a free chart the matrix of multiplication by $b\otimes1$ is obtained by applying the scalar ring map to every entry of the matrix for $b$. The permutation-sum formula for the determinant [def-weil-endomorphism-determinant] therefore gives $N(b)\otimes1=N(b\otimes1)$. The same calculation holds after any substitution in a polynomial ring. It holds globally since the pulled-back free charts cover and the norm sections restrict to these determinants. No freeness on the whole affine scheme or constant rank is needed.

source.place: Tag 03BL norm argument; Tag 03BH uses compatibility with base change; determinant construction in Divisors Tag 0BD2

proof.text: For any $f\in A'$ write $f=\sum_{j=1}^m a_j'\otimes\lambda_j$ and put $F=\sum_j a_j'T_j\in A[T_1,\ldots,T_m]$. Extend the original groupoid by adjoining these same polynomial variables to both rings. This is its product with affine $m$-space over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$, hence still a groupoid with finite locally free source and target (finite, flat and locally finite presentation are preserved separately as in step 3). Apply [lem-a1-affine-groupoid-invariant-norm] to obtain $G=N_{\sigma[T]}(\tau[T](F))\in C[T_1,\ldots,T_m]$: polynomial source and target images agree exactly when their coefficients agree. Substitute $a\mapsto a\otimes1$ and $T_j\mapsto1\otimes\lambda_j$. By step 4 the resulting element is $g=N_{\sigma'}(\tau'(f))\in A'$. Since every coefficient of $G$ belongs to $C$, this substitution sends $G$ to the scalar $c[T](G)(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m)\in k\subset A'$. Consequently $\alpha_0(g)=\alpha_1(g)$. This proves the needed scalar equality for these particular norms directly, without assuming invariants commute with nonflat scalar extension.

source.place: Tag 03BL norm argument; polynomial lifting as in the proof of Tag 03BK (groupoids-lemma-invariants-base-change), (2)(a)

proof.text: Let $D_1=B'\otimes_{A',\alpha_1}k$, using $\sigma'$ for the $A'$-algebra structure. The affine tensor formula identifies $\operatorname{Spec}D_1$ with the source fibre of $s'$ over $\alpha_1$. It is finite-dimensional over $k$ by tensoring finite module generators of $B'$; hence its structure morphism is finite and it has finitely many points by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-closed-map-finite-fibres]. Finite implies integral by [pqf-lem-finite-integral-lft], and every prime over the maximal ideal $(0)$ of $k$ is maximal by [lem-weil-pbc-integral-prime-over-maximal-maximal]. Also $D_1$ is finitely generated as a $k$-algebra (a finite module generating set already generates it as an algebra), so [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base] gives residue field $k$ at each of these closed points. Thus the points correspond to a finite list of all $k$-algebra maps $\beta_i:B'\to k$ with $\beta_i\sigma'=\alpha_1$. This list is nonempty because it contains the identity arrow at $\alpha_1$.

source.place: Tag 03BL, paragraph beginning Since s is finite

proof.text: Suppose no arrow has source $\alpha_1$ and target $\alpha_0$. For the finite list in step 6 put $\alpha_i'=\beta_i\tau'$, $\mathfrak m_i=\ker\alpha_i'$ and $\mathfrak m_0=\ker\alpha_0$. These kernels are maximal because all the maps are $k$-algebra maps to $k$, hence surjective. The kernels are unequal: two such maps with the same kernel identify the quotient with $k$ identically on its subfield $k$, so are equal, contrary to the assumption. Distinct maximal ideals do not contain each other, so $\mathfrak m_0\not\subset\mathfrak m_i$ for each $i$. Prime avoidance [lem-weil-pbc-prime-avoidance] therefore supplies $f\in\mathfrak m_0$ outside all $\mathfrak m_i$. Equivalently, $\alpha_0(f)=0$ whereas $\alpha_i'(f)\ne0$ for every $i$.

source.place: Tag 03BL, prime-avoidance paragraph, referring to Algebra Tag 00DS

proof.text: Apply the local norm prime criterion [lem-pd-finite-free-norm-prime-criterion] to $\tau'(f)$. More explicitly, choose a free affine norm chart around the point $\ker\alpha_1$; restriction does not change its source fibre, so all primes over this point are the points listed in step 6. At each of them the value of $\tau'(f)$ is $\beta_i\tau'(f)=\alpha_i'(f)\ne0$. The criterion and the chart description of the norm imply $\alpha_1(g)\ne0$ for $g=N_{\sigma'}(\tau'(f))$. Around $\ker\alpha_0$ use another free norm chart. The identity arrow at $\alpha_0$ is a prime in its source fibre and evaluates $\tau'(f)$ to $\alpha_0(f)=0$. The same criterion gives $\alpha_0(g)=0$. This contradicts the scalar equality in step 5. Thus an arrow with source $\alpha_1$ and target $\alpha_0$ exists.

source.place: Tag 03BL, norm nonvanishing argument; its determinant references are supplied by the cited norm-prime criterion

proof.text: A $k$-arrow in the scalar-extended groupoid gives an original $k$-arrow by precomposing $B\to B'$. Conversely an original $k$-arrow $\gamma:B\to k$ whose endpoints restrict to $c$ extends by $b\otimes\lambda\mapsto\gamma(b)\lambda$, so step 8 gives an arrow relating any two original lifts. An arrow always preserves the restrictions to $C$ since $\sigma|_C=\tau|_C$. Identity, inverse and composition in $R(k)\rightrightarrows U(k)$ make the relation of being joined by one arrow reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Therefore it equals the equivalence relation generated by $s,t$, and steps 2 and 8 prove exactly the surjectivity and fibre assertion on $k$-points.

Finally let $u_0,u_1\in|U|$ have the same image $m\in|M|$. By integrality and [lem-a1-integral-residue-extension-algebraic], both $\kappa(u_j)/\kappa(m)$ are algebraic. Choose an algebraic closure $k$ of $\kappa(m)$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. By [lem-weil-pbc-algebraic-extension-embeds-algebraically-closed] embed both residue fields into this same $k$, extending its fixed inclusion of $\kappa(m)$. The composites $A\to\kappa(u_j)\to k$ have underlying points $u_j$ and the same restriction $C\to\kappa(m)\to k$. By step 9 they are joined by a $k$-arrow. Its underlying point in $R$ has the two required endpoints; invert the arrow if necessary to match the order $s(r)=u_0$, $t(r)=u_1$. Conversely, an underlying point $r\in|R|$ has equal $M$-images under $s,t$, since the two ring maps $C\to B$ are equal. Together with step 1 this proves the entire assertion on ordinary points.
